sections.title: Two ways to multiply two vectors

board_events.text: Two ways to multiply two vectors
One asks 'how much do they agree in direction?' and answers with a number (dot product).
The other asks 'how much do they spread apart?' and answers with a new vector (cross product).
Dot: maximal when parallel, zero when perpendicular.
Cross: zero when parallel, maximal when perpendicular.
Wherever one is large, the other tends to be small, mirror-image questions.
Together they fix how two vectors are oriented relative to each other.
Master both and you own most of the chapter's marks.

segments.text: <curious>Here is a question you might not have asked: how do you multiply two vectors? It turns out there are two completely different answers.
The first multiplication asks, how much do these two vectors agree in direction? And it answers with a plain number, the dot, or scalar, product.
The second asks, how much do these two vectors spread apart? And it answers with a brand new vector, the cross, or vector, product.
The dot product is largest when the vectors point the same way, and it drops to zero when they are perpendicular.
The cross product is the exact opposite, zero when they are parallel, and largest when they cross at a right angle.
So they are mirror-image questions: wherever one is large, the other tends to be small.
Between them, these two products tell you everything about how two vectors are oriented relative to each other.
This is one of the highest-yield subtopics in the chapter, so master both products and you own most of its marks.
<curious>एक सवाल जो शायद आपने नहीं पूछा: दो vectors को multiply कैसे करते हैं? पता चलता है कि इसके दो completely different जवाब हैं।
पहली multiplication पूछती है, ये दो vectors direction में कितना agree करते हैं? और जवाब देती है एक plain number से, dot, या scalar, product.
दूसरी पूछती है, ये दो vectors कितना spread apart होते हैं? और जवाब देती है एक brand new vector से, cross, या vector, product.
Dot product सबसे बड़ा तब होता है जब vectors same way point करें, और zero हो जाता है जब वो perpendicular हों।
Cross product बिल्कुल opposite है, parallel होने पर zero, और right angle पर सबसे बड़ा।
तो ये mirror-image questions हैं: जहाँ एक बड़ा होता है, वहाँ दूसरा छोटा होता है।
इन दोनों के बीच, ये products आपको बता देते हैं कि दो vectors एक दूसरे के relative कैसे oriented हैं।
ये chapter का सबसे high-yield subtopics में से एक है, तो दोनों products master कर लो और इसके ज़्यादातर marks आपके।

board_events.text: The dot product: overlap
Push a handcart down a lane at a slight angle.
Only the part of your push ALONG the lane moves the cart forward.
The dot product measures that useful overlap between two directions.
Same direction: maximum overlap. Perpendicular: zero overlap.
The result is a single number, 'amount of agreement' is a quantity, not a direction.

board_events.caption: The dot product is the shadow one vector casts on another.

board_events.text: Think of it as the shadow one vector casts on another.

segments.text: Let us build real intuition for the dot product, because a formula without a picture is easy to forget.
Picture pushing a loaded handcart, a thela, down a straight market lane, and you shove at a slight angle to the lane.
Only the part of your push that points along the lane actually moves the cart forward; the sideways part is completely wasted.
The dot product measures exactly that useful overlap between two directions, how much of one lines up with the other.
When the two vectors point the same way the overlap is maximum, and when they are perpendicular there is no overlap at all, so the dot product is zero.
And crucially the result is a single number, a scalar, because amount of agreement is just a quantity, not a direction.
On the board you can see vector a dropping a perpendicular shadow onto vector b, and that shadow length is the heart of the dot product.
So carry this image: the dot product is the shadow one vector casts on another.
Dot product के लिए असली intuition बनाते हैं, क्योंकि picture के बिना formula भूलना आसान है।
सोचिए एक loaded handcart, एक thela, को सीधी market lane में push कर रहे हैं, और आप lane से थोड़ा angle पर धक्का देते हैं।
आपके push का सिर्फ वो हिस्सा जो lane के along है, actually cart को आगे बढ़ाता है; sideways हिस्सा पूरी तरह waste है।
Dot product ठीक वही useful overlap measure करता है दो directions के बीच, कि एक दूसरे से कितना line up करता है।
जब दोनों vectors same way point करें overlap maximum होता है, और जब perpendicular हों तो कोई overlap नहीं, तो dot product zero।
और crucially result एक single number है, एक scalar, क्योंकि amount of agreement बस एक quantity है, direction नहीं।
Board पर देखिए vector a, vector b पर एक perpendicular shadow गिरा रहा है, वो shadow length ही dot product का दिल है।
तो ये image साथ रखिए: dot product वो shadow है जो एक vector दूसरे पर डालता है।

sections.title: The cross product: spread and twist

board_events.text: The cross product: spread and twist
Open a heavy almirah door: push near the hinge, little turn; push at the far edge, big turn.
The turning effect is largest when your push is perpendicular to the door.
The cross product is zero when vectors are parallel, maximal when perpendicular.
It produces a NEW vector, perpendicular to both, along the axis of their spread.
Right-hand rule: curl fingers from a to b; the thumb points along $\vec a \times \vec b$.
$\vec a \times \vec b = -\,\vec b \times \vec a$, reverse the order and the thumb flips.

board_events.caption: a and b lie in a plane; a x b stands perpendicular, along the axis of spread.

segments.text: The cross product needs a different picture, think of turning, not overlap.
Picture opening a heavy almirah door. Push right next to the hinge and almost nothing happens; push at the far edge, perpendicular to the door, and it swings open easily.
So the turning effect depends on how perpendicular your push is to the door, and it is strongest at a right angle.
The cross product captures exactly this: it is zero when the two vectors are parallel, and largest when they are perpendicular.
But unlike the dot product it produces a brand new vector, one pointing perpendicular to both, straight along the axis of their spread, like the hinge sticking out of the door.
Its direction is fixed by the right-hand rule: curl the fingers of your right hand from a toward b, and your thumb points along a cross b.
And here is why order matters: reverse it, and your thumb flips, so a cross b equals minus b cross a.
On the board, a and b lie in the flat plane while a cross b stands straight up out of it, that is the whole geometry.
Cross product को अलग picture चाहिए, turning सोचिए, overlap नहीं।
एक heavy almirah door खोलना सोचिए। Hinge के बिल्कुल पास push करो तो कुछ नहीं होता; far edge पर, door के perpendicular, push करो तो वो आसानी से swing हो जाता है।
तो turning effect इस पर depend करता है कि आपका push door के कितना perpendicular है, और right angle पर सबसे strong होता है।
Cross product ठीक यही capture करता है: parallel होने पर zero, और perpendicular होने पर सबसे बड़ा।
पर dot product के उलट ये एक brand new vector बनाता है, जो दोनों के perpendicular होता है, सीधा उनके spread के axis के साथ, जैसे door से बाहर निकला hinge.
इसकी direction right-hand rule से fix होती है: right hand की fingers a से b की तरफ curl करो, और आपका thumb a cross b के साथ point करता है।
और यहाँ order क्यों matter करता है: उल्टा करो, thumb flip हो जाता है, तो a cross b equals minus b cross a.
Board पर a और b flat plane में हैं जबकि a cross b उससे सीधा ऊपर खड़ा है, यही पूरी geometry है।

sections.title: Four traps in the two products

board_events.text: Four traps in the two products
For non-zero vectors, $\vec a \cdot \vec b = 0$ means perpendicular.
But $\vec a \times \vec b = \vec 0$ means parallel (collinear).
Confusing these two zero-conditions is the single most common error here.
The cross product is NOT commutative: $\vec a \times \vec b = -\,\vec b \times \vec a$.
There is no vector division; from $\vec a \cdot \vec b$ alone you cannot recover $\vec b$.
A scalar vs a vector: $\vec a \cdot \vec b$ is a number; $\vec a \times \vec b$ is a vector.
Write one where the other belongs and it is a conceptual, not arithmetic, slip.

segments.text: Before the formulas, four traps that this subtopic sets again and again.
First, the word zero means opposite things for the two products. For non-zero vectors, a dot b equal to zero means the vectors are perpendicular.
But a cross b equal to the zero vector means the vectors are parallel, or collinear.
Confusing these two zero-conditions is, truly, the single most common error in the whole subtopic.
Second, the cross product is not commutative, a cross b equals minus b cross a, while the dot product is commutative.
Third, there is no such thing as vector division. From the number a dot b alone, you simply cannot recover the vector b.
Fourth, keep the outputs straight: a dot b is a number, a scalar, while a cross b is a vector.
Writing one where the other belongs, saying a dot b is a vector for instance, is a conceptual mistake, not just an arithmetic one.
Formulas से पहले, चार traps जो ये subtopic बार बार सेट करता है।
पहला, word zero दोनों products के लिए opposite चीज़ें मतलब रखता है। Non-zero vectors के लिए, a dot b equal to zero मतलब vectors perpendicular हैं।
पर a cross b equal to zero vector मतलब vectors parallel, या collinear, हैं।
इन दो zero-conditions को confuse करना, सच में, पूरे subtopic की सबसे common error है।
दूसरा, cross product commutative नहीं है, a cross b equals minus b cross a, जबकि dot product commutative है।
तीसरा, vector division जैसी कोई चीज़ नहीं है। सिर्फ number a dot b से, आप vector b recover नहीं कर सकते।
चौथा, outputs सीधे रखो: a dot b एक number है, scalar, जबकि a cross b एक vector है।
एक को दूसरे की जगह लिखना, जैसे कहना a dot b एक vector है, ये conceptual mistake है, सिर्फ arithmetic नहीं।

board_events.text: Dot product: definition and components
For vectors with angle $\theta$ between them, where $0 \le \theta \le \pi$:
Component form for $\vec a = a_1\hat i + a_2\hat j + a_3\hat k$ and similarly $\vec b$:

board_events.latex: \vec a \cdot \vec b = a_1 b_1 + a_2 b_2 + a_3 b_3

board_events.text: The result is a scalar, a single number.
Basis: $\hat i \cdot \hat i = 1$ and $\hat i \cdot \hat j = 0$, and so on.

segments.text: Now the precise definitions, starting with the dot product, in two equivalent forms.
Take two vectors with an angle theta between them, where theta runs from zero to pi.
The geometric definition is a dot b equals the magnitude of a, times the magnitude of b, times cosine theta.
For calculation we prefer components. Write a as a-one i-hat plus a-two j-hat plus a-three k-hat, and b similarly.
Then a dot b is simply a-one b-one plus a-two b-two plus a-three b-three, multiply matching components and add.
Notice the result is a scalar, a single number, exactly as the overlap picture promised.
A neat special case: a dotted with itself gives the magnitude of a, squared, since the angle is zero and cosine is one.
And the basis rule underneath it all: i-hat dot i-hat is one, while i-hat dot j-hat is zero, and so on for every pair.
अब precise definitions, dot product से शुरू, दो equivalent forms में।
दो vectors लो जिनके बीच angle theta है, जहाँ theta zero से pi तक चलता है।
Geometric definition है a dot b equals magnitude of a, times magnitude of b, times cosine theta.
Calculation के लिए हम components prefer करते हैं। a को लिखो a-one i-hat plus a-two j-hat plus a-three k-hat, और b वैसे ही।
तो a dot b बस है a-one b-one plus a-two b-two plus a-three b-three, matching components multiply करके add करो।
ध्यान दो result एक scalar है, एक single number, ठीक जैसा overlap picture ने promise किया था।
एक neat special case: a को खुद से dot करो तो मिलता है magnitude of a, squared, क्योंकि angle zero है तो cosine one।
और सबके नीचे basis rule: i-hat dot i-hat है one, जबकि i-hat dot j-hat है zero, और हर pair के लिए वैसे ही।

board_events.text: Angle between vectors, and projection
Rearrange the definition to read the angle:
Scalar projection of $\vec a$ on $\vec b$, how much of a lies along b:
Projection VECTOR (with direction): $\dfrac{\vec a \cdot \vec b}{|\vec b|^2}\,\vec b$.
Divide by the vector you project ONTO, its magnitude, not the other's.

board_events.caption: a casts a shadow on b; that shadow length is the scalar projection.

segments.text: The dot product immediately hands us two everyday tools: the angle between vectors, and the projection of one onto another.
For the angle, just rearrange the definition to solve for cosine theta.
Cosine theta equals a dot b, divided by the product of the two magnitudes, compute the dot product, divide, take the inverse cosine.
For the projection, we ask how much of a lies along the direction of b.
The scalar projection of a on b is a dot b, divided by the magnitude of b, one clean number.
If you want the projection as a vector, keeping its direction, multiply by b over the magnitude of b squared, the same overlap, now pointing along b.
<whisper>And here is the slip to guard against, you divide by the magnitude of the vector you are projecting onto, not the one being projected.
On the board a casts its shadow onto b, and the length of that shadow is exactly the scalar projection.
Dot product तुरंत हमें दो everyday tools देता है: vectors के बीच angle, और एक का दूसरे पर projection.
Angle के लिए, बस definition को rearrange करके cosine theta निकालो।
Cosine theta equals a dot b, divided by दोनों magnitudes का product, dot product compute करो, divide करो, inverse cosine ले लो।
Projection के लिए हम पूछते हैं कि a का कितना हिस्सा b की direction के along है।
Scalar projection of a on b है a dot b, divided by magnitude of b, एक clean number।
अगर projection vector चाहिए, direction के साथ, तो b over magnitude of b squared से multiply करो, वही overlap, अब b के along pointing।
<whisper>और यहाँ जिस slip से बचना है, आप उस vector की magnitude से divide करते हो जिस पर project कर रहे हो, projected वाले से नहीं।
Board पर a अपनी shadow b पर डालता है, और उस shadow की length ठीक scalar projection है।

sections.title: Key properties of the dot product

board_events.text: Key properties of the dot product
Commutative: $\vec a \cdot \vec b = \vec b \cdot \vec a$.
Distributive: $\vec a \cdot (\vec b + \vec c) = \vec a \cdot \vec b + \vec a \cdot \vec c$.
Perpendicularity: for non-zero vectors, $\vec a \cdot \vec b = 0 \iff \vec a \perp \vec b$.
A zero dot product is the cleanest test for a right angle.
Sign reads the angle: positive is acute, zero is right, negative is obtuse.
These few rules let you manipulate dot products like ordinary algebra.

segments.text: Let us collect the working properties of the dot product, the rules you will lean on in every problem.
It is commutative: a dot b equals b dot a, so order never matters for the dot product.
It is distributive over addition: a dot the quantity b plus c splits into a dot b plus a dot c.
A vector dotted with itself gives its magnitude squared, worth memorising, because it turns lengths into dot products.
The perpendicularity test: for non-zero vectors, a dot b equals zero if and only if a is perpendicular to b.
That makes a zero dot product the cleanest possible test for a right angle.
And the sign alone reads the angle for you, positive means acute, zero means a right angle, negative means obtuse.
Armed with these few rules, you can push dot products around just like ordinary algebra.
Dot product की working properties इकट्ठा करते हैं, वो rules जिन पर हर problem में भरोसा करोगे।
ये commutative है: a dot b equals b dot a, तो dot product के लिए order कभी matter नहीं करता।
ये addition पर distributive है: a dot the quantity b plus c टूट कर बनता है a dot b plus a dot c.
एक vector को खुद से dot करो तो magnitude squared मिलता है, याद रखने लायक, क्योंकि ये lengths को dot products में बदल देता है।
Perpendicularity test: non-zero vectors के लिए, a dot b equals zero if and only if a, b के perpendicular है।
इससे zero dot product right angle का सबसे clean test बन जाता है।
और अकेला sign ही आपके लिए angle पढ़ देता है, positive मतलब acute, zero मतलब right angle, negative मतलब obtuse.
इन कुछ rules के साथ, आप dot products को ordinary algebra की तरह push कर सकते हो।

board_events.text: Cross product: definition and determinant
With $\hat n$ the unit vector perpendicular to both (right-hand rule):
Magnitude alone: $|\vec a \times \vec b| = |\vec a|\,|\vec b|\sin\theta$.
Determinant (component) form:

board_events.latex: \vec a \times \vec b = \begin{vmatrix} \hat i & \hat j & \hat k \\ a_1 & a_2 & a_3 \\ b_1 & b_2 & b_3 \end{vmatrix}
\vec a \times \vec b = (a_2 b_3 - a_3 b_2)\hat i - (a_1 b_3 - a_3 b_1)\hat j + (a_1 b_2 - a_2 b_1)\hat k

board_events.text: The result is a vector; the middle ($\hat j$) term carries a minus sign.

segments.text: Now the cross product in symbols, both its geometric definition and the determinant you will actually compute with.
Let n-hat be the unit vector perpendicular to both a and b, with its direction set by the right-hand rule.
Then a cross b equals the magnitude of a, times the magnitude of b, times sine theta, all times n-hat.
If you only need the size, drop the n-hat: the magnitude of a cross b is the magnitude of a, times the magnitude of b, times sine theta.
For computation we use the determinant form, and this is the workhorse of the whole subtopic.
Write a three by three determinant with i-hat, j-hat, k-hat across the top row, the components of a in the second row, and the components of b in the third.
Expanding along the top gives the standard result, the i term, minus the j term, plus the k term, each a little two by two cross-difference.
<whisper>Burn this into memory, the middle term, the j-hat term, carries a minus sign. That single minus is the most common cross-product slip in exams.
अब cross product symbols में, इसकी geometric definition और वो determinant जिससे आप actually compute करोगे।
n-hat को दोनों a और b के perpendicular unit vector मानो, जिसकी direction right-hand rule से set होती है।
तो a cross b equals magnitude of a, times magnitude of b, times sine theta, all times n-hat.
अगर सिर्फ size चाहिए, n-hat हटा दो: magnitude of a cross b है magnitude of a, times magnitude of b, times sine theta.
Computation के लिए हम determinant form use करते हैं, और यही पूरे subtopic का workhorse है।
एक three by three determinant लिखो, top row में i-hat, j-hat, k-hat, दूसरी row में a के components, और तीसरी में b के।
Top के along expand करने पर standard result मिलता है, i term, minus j term, plus k term, हर एक एक छोटा two by two cross-difference.
<whisper>ये memory में जला लो, middle term, j-hat term, minus sign carry करता है। वो एक minus exams में सबसे common cross-product slip है।

board_events.text: Cross product geometry: areas
The magnitude $|\vec a \times \vec b|$ equals the area of the parallelogram framed by a and b.
Unit vector perpendicular to both a and b:
The $\pm$ is real: two opposite normals are both perpendicular to the plane.

board_events.caption: a and b span a parallelogram whose area is the cross-product magnitude.

segments.text: The cross product is not just an abstract vector, its magnitude is literally an area, and that makes it a geometry powerhouse.
If a and b are two adjacent sides drawn from a corner, the magnitude of a cross b equals the area of the parallelogram they frame.
So the parallelogram area is simply the magnitude of a cross b.
And a triangle is half a parallelogram, so a triangle with sides a and b from one vertex has area one half the magnitude of a cross b.
The cross product also hands you a direction perpendicular to both vectors at once.
The unit vector perpendicular to both is plus or minus a cross b, divided by its own magnitude.
That plus or minus is genuine: the plane has two opposite normals, and both are perpendicular to it, so both answers are valid.
On the board, a and b span the parallelogram whose area is that magnitude, with the perpendicular standing out of the plane.
Cross product सिर्फ एक abstract vector नहीं है, इसकी magnitude literally एक area है, और यही इसे geometry powerhouse बनाता है।
अगर a और b एक corner से खींची दो adjacent sides हैं, तो magnitude of a cross b उस parallelogram का area है जो वो frame करती हैं।
तो parallelogram area बस magnitude of a cross b है।
और triangle, parallelogram का आधा है, तो एक vertex से sides a और b वाले triangle का area है one half the magnitude of a cross b.
Cross product आपको एक साथ दोनों vectors के perpendicular direction भी दे देता है।
दोनों के perpendicular unit vector है plus or minus a cross b, divided by उसकी अपनी magnitude।
वो plus or minus genuine है: plane के दो opposite normals होते हैं, और दोनों उसके perpendicular हैं, तो दोनों answers valid हैं।
Board पर a और b वो parallelogram span करते हैं जिसका area वही magnitude है, perpendicular plane से बाहर खड़ा।

sections.title: Cross product properties and the complementary pair

board_events.text: Cross product properties and the complementary pair
Anti-commutative: $\vec a \times \vec b = -\,\vec b \times \vec a$.
Distributive: $\vec a \times (\vec b + \vec c) = \vec a \times \vec b + \vec a \times \vec c$.
Parallelism: for non-zero vectors, $\vec a \times \vec b = \vec 0 \iff \vec a \parallel \vec b$.
Basis (cyclic): $\hat i \times \hat j = \hat k$, $\hat j \times \hat k = \hat i$, $\hat k \times \hat i = \hat j$.
Dot peaks at $\theta = 0$; cross peaks at $\theta = 90^\circ$, perfectly complementary.

board_events.caption: cos (dot) falls while sin (cross) rises; they cross at 45 degrees.

segments.text: Now the working properties of the cross product, ending with the beautiful way it complements the dot product.
It is anti-commutative: a cross b equals minus b cross a, the sign flip we saw from the right-hand rule.
It is distributive over addition, just like the dot product: a cross the quantity b plus c splits into two cross products.
A vector crossed with itself is the zero vector, because the angle is zero and sine zero is zero.
The parallelism test: for non-zero vectors, a cross b equals the zero vector if and only if a is parallel to b.
The basis rule is cyclic: i cross j is k, j cross k is i, k cross i is j, and reversing any pair flips the sign.
Step back and see the harmony: the dot product peaks at zero degrees, while the cross magnitude peaks at ninety degrees.
<excited>On the board those two curves, cosine falling and sine rising, cross exactly at forty five degrees, a perfect complementary pair.
अब cross product की working properties, और अंत में वो beautiful तरीका जिससे ये dot product को complement करता है।
ये anti-commutative है: a cross b equals minus b cross a, वही sign flip जो right-hand rule से देखा।
ये addition पर distributive है, बिल्कुल dot product की तरह: a cross the quantity b plus c दो cross products में टूट जाता है।
एक vector को खुद से cross करो तो zero vector मिलता है, क्योंकि angle zero है और sine zero, zero है।
Parallelism test: non-zero vectors के लिए, a cross b equals zero vector if and only if a, b के parallel है।
Basis rule cyclic है: i cross j है k, j cross k है i, k cross i है j, और किसी भी pair को reverse करने पर sign flip।
पीछे हट कर harmony देखो: dot product zero degrees पर peak करता है, जबकि cross magnitude ninety degrees पर।
<excited>Board पर वो दो curves, cosine गिरती और sine चढ़ती, exactly forty five degrees पर cross करती हैं, एक perfect complementary pair.

sections.title: Proof: the component formula for the dot product

board_events.text: Proof: the component formula for the dot product
Claim: $\vec a \cdot \vec b = a_1 b_1 + a_2 b_2 + a_3 b_3$.
Write both vectors in components and use distributivity.
The product expands into nine basis dot products $\hat e_p \cdot \hat e_q$.
Basis rule: $\hat e_p \cdot \hat e_q = 1$ if $p=q$, and $0$ otherwise.
Every cross term with $p \neq q$ dies, leaving only three diagonal terms.

board_events.latex: \vec a \cdot \vec b = a_1 b_1 + a_2 b_2 + a_3 b_3

board_events.text: The whole formula is just the basis rule doing the bookkeeping.

segments.text: Let us prove why the neat component formula for the dot product is true, it flows straight from distributivity.
The claim is that a dot b equals a-one b-one plus a-two b-two plus a-three b-three.
Start by writing both vectors in components, and remember the dot product distributes over sums.
Multiplying the two bracketed expressions produces nine basis dot products, every i, j, k of a dotted with every i, j, k of b.
Now invoke the basis rule: a basis vector dotted with itself gives one, and dotted with a different basis vector gives zero.
So every cross term, where the two basis vectors differ, simply dies, and only the three diagonal terms survive.
Those survivors are a-one b-one plus a-two b-two plus a-three b-three, exactly the component formula.
The whole proof is really just the orthonormal basis rule quietly doing the bookkeeping for us.
Prove करते हैं कि dot product का neat component formula सच क्यों है, ये सीधे distributivity से निकलता है।
Claim ये है कि a dot b equals a-one b-one plus a-two b-two plus a-three b-three.
दोनों vectors को components में लिखो, और याद रखो dot product sums पर distribute करता है।
दोनों bracketed expressions को multiply करने पर nine basis dot products बनते हैं, a के हर i, j, k को b के हर i, j, k से dot।
अब basis rule लगाओ: एक basis vector को खुद से dot करो तो one, और अलग basis vector से dot करो तो zero।
तो हर cross term, जहाँ दोनों basis vectors अलग हैं, बस मर जाता है, और सिर्फ तीन diagonal terms बचते हैं।
वो survivors हैं a-one b-one plus a-two b-two plus a-three b-three, बिल्कुल component formula।
पूरा proof असल में बस orthonormal basis rule है जो चुपचाप हमारे लिए bookkeeping कर रहा है।

sections.title: Proof: the determinant formula for the cross product

board_events.text: Proof: the determinant formula for the cross product
Expand $\vec a \times \vec b$ by distributivity over nine basis cross products.
Three terms $\hat i \times \hat i$, $\hat j \times \hat j$, $\hat k \times \hat k$ equal $\vec 0$.
The other six pair up via the cyclic rules $\hat i \times \hat j = \hat k$, and so on.

board_events.latex: \vec a \times \vec b = (a_2 b_3 - a_3 b_2)\hat i + (a_3 b_1 - a_1 b_3)\hat j + (a_1 b_2 - a_2 b_1)\hat k

board_events.text: This is exactly the cofactor expansion of the $3\times3$ determinant along its top row.
The determinant's antisymmetry reproduces $\vec a \times \vec b = -\,\vec b \times \vec a$ for free.
So the determinant is not a trick, it is the algebra, packaged neatly.

segments.text: Now we show that the tidy determinant for the cross product is not a memory trick but a genuine consequence of the basis rules.
Expand a cross b using distributivity, so the product of the two component sums splits into nine basis cross products.
Three of those nine, i cross i, j cross j, and k cross k, are each the zero vector, so they drop out.
The remaining six pair up neatly under the cyclic rules: i cross j is k, j cross k is i, k cross i is j, with the reverses carrying a minus sign.
Collecting the survivors gives a cross b as a-two b-three minus a-three b-two along i, plus a-three b-one minus a-one b-three along j, plus a-one b-two minus a-two b-one along k.
And that expression is precisely the cofactor expansion of the three by three determinant along its top row.
There is a bonus, the determinant is antisymmetric in its last two rows, so swapping a and b flips the sign automatically, reproducing a cross b equals minus b cross a.
So the determinant is not a shortcut to memorise blindly; it is the algebra itself, packaged into one neat grid.
अब दिखाते हैं कि cross product का tidy determinant कोई memory trick नहीं, बल्कि basis rules का genuine consequence है।
a cross b को distributivity से expand करो, तो दोनों component sums का product nine basis cross products में टूट जाता है।
उन nine में से तीन, i cross i, j cross j, और k cross k, हर एक zero vector है, तो वो निकल जाते हैं।
बाकी छह cyclic rules के तहत neatly pair हो जाते हैं: i cross j है k, j cross k है i, k cross i है j, और reverses minus sign carry करते हैं।
Survivors इकट्ठा करने पर a cross b मिलता है, a-two b-three minus a-three b-two along i, plus a-three b-one minus a-one b-three along j, plus a-one b-two minus a-two b-one along k.
और वो expression ठीक three by three determinant का cofactor expansion है top row के along।
एक bonus है, determinant अपनी last two rows में antisymmetric है, तो a और b swap करने पर sign apne आप flip होता है, a cross b equals minus b cross a reproduce करता है।
तो determinant कोई shortcut नहीं जिसे blindly रटो; ये algebra खुद है, एक neat grid में packaged।

board_events.text: Proof: Lagrange's identity
Claim: $(\vec a \cdot \vec b)^2 + |\vec a \times \vec b|^2 = |\vec a|^2 |\vec b|^2$.
Let $\theta$ be the angle. Then $\vec a \cdot \vec b = |\vec a||\vec b|\cos\theta$.
And $|\vec a \times \vec b| = |\vec a||\vec b|\sin\theta$.

board_events.latex: (\vec a \cdot \vec b)^2 + |\vec a \times \vec b|^2 = |\vec a|^2|\vec b|^2(\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta)
(\vec a \cdot \vec b)^2 + |\vec a \times \vec b|^2 = |\vec a|^2|\vec b|^2

board_events.text: The Pythagorean identity $\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta = 1$ closes it.
Payoff: get $|\vec a \times \vec b|$ from $\vec a \cdot \vec b$ without ever finding the angle.

segments.text: This proof ties the two products together with one elegant identity, Lagrange's identity.
The claim: the square of a dot b, plus the square of the magnitude of a cross b, equals the magnitude of a squared times the magnitude of b squared.
Let theta be the angle between them. Then a dot b is the two magnitudes times cosine theta.
And the magnitude of a cross b is the two magnitudes times sine theta.
Square each and add. Both terms share the factor magnitude of a squared, times magnitude of b squared, leaving cosine squared theta plus sine squared theta.
But cosine squared plus sine squared is one, so the sum is just the magnitude of a squared, times the magnitude of b squared.
The whole proof hinges on that one Pythagorean identity quietly closing the gap.
<whisper>And here is the exam payoff, you can find the magnitude of a cross b directly from a dot b, without ever computing the angle.
ये proof दोनों products को एक elegant identity से जोड़ देता है, Lagrange's identity.
Claim: a dot b का square, plus magnitude of a cross b का square, equals magnitude of a squared times magnitude of b squared.
theta को उनके बीच का angle मानो। तो a dot b है दोनों magnitudes times cosine theta.
और magnitude of a cross b है दोनों magnitudes times sine theta.
हर एक को square करके add करो। दोनों terms में common factor है magnitude of a squared, times magnitude of b squared, बचता है cosine squared theta plus sine squared theta.
पर cosine squared plus sine squared है one, तो sum बस magnitude of a squared, times magnitude of b squared है।
पूरा proof उसी एक Pythagorean identity पर टिका है जो चुपचाप gap बंद कर देती है।
<whisper>और यहाँ exam payoff, आप magnitude of a cross b सीधे a dot b से निकाल सकते हो, angle कभी compute किए बिना।

board_events.text: Example: dot product, angle, projection
$\vec a = 2\hat i + 3\hat j + \hat k$, $\vec b = \hat i - 2\hat j + 2\hat k$. Find $\vec a \cdot \vec b$, the angle, and proj of a on b.
Magnitudes: $|\vec a| = \sqrt{14}$, $|\vec b| = 3$.
Negative dot product, obtuse angle, negative projection, all consistent.
One dot product feeds all three answers.

segments.text: Let us run a clean board-level problem that uses the dot product for three things at once.
We have a equals two i-hat plus three j-hat plus k-hat, and b equals i-hat minus two j-hat plus two k-hat, and we want the dot product, the angle, and the projection of a on b.
The dot product first: two times one, plus three times minus two, plus one times two, that is two minus six plus two, which is minus two.
For the angle we need magnitudes. The magnitude of a is root fourteen, and the magnitude of b is root of one plus four plus four, which is three.
So cosine theta is minus two over three root fourteen, and theta is the inverse cosine of that, an obtuse angle, since the cosine is negative.
The projection of a on b is the dot product over the magnitude of b, which is minus two over three.
Notice everything agrees: the negative dot product signals an obtuse angle, and that same negativity shows up in the projection.
So a single dot product quietly fed all three answers, that is the efficiency you want in the exam.
एक clean board-level problem चलाते हैं जो dot product को एक साथ तीन चीज़ों के लिए use करती है।
हमारे पास a equals two i-hat plus three j-hat plus k-hat, और b equals i-hat minus two j-hat plus two k-hat, और चाहिए dot product, angle, और projection of a on b.
पहले dot product: two times one, plus three times minus two, plus one times two, यानी two minus six plus two, जो minus two है।
Angle के लिए magnitudes चाहिए। Magnitude of a है root fourteen, और magnitude of b है root of one plus four plus four, जो three है।
तो cosine theta है minus two over three root fourteen, और theta उसका inverse cosine है, एक obtuse angle, क्योंकि cosine negative है।
Projection of a on b है dot product over magnitude of b, जो minus two over three है।
ध्यान दो सब कुछ agree करता है: negative dot product obtuse angle signal करता है, और वही negativity projection में दिखती है।
तो एक single dot product ने चुपचाप तीनों answers feed कर दिए, यही efficiency आपको exam में चाहिए।

board_events.text: Example: perpendicular vs parallel
$\vec a = \lambda\hat i + 2\hat j - 3\hat k$, $\vec b = 3\hat i - \hat j + 2\hat k$. Find $\lambda$ for (i) perpendicular, (ii) parallel.
Trap: perpendicular uses the DOT; parallel uses proportional components.
(i) Perpendicular means $\vec a \cdot \vec b = 0$:
(ii) Parallel means components proportional: $\dfrac{\lambda}{3} = \dfrac{2}{-1} = \dfrac{-3}{2}$.
The last two are unequal, so NO $\lambda$ makes them parallel.

segments.text: This example is really a test of whether you know which product goes with which condition.
We have a equals lambda i-hat plus two j-hat minus three k-hat, and b equals three i-hat minus j-hat plus two k-hat, and we want lambda for perpendicular, then for parallel.
<whisper>Here is the trap, students reach for the same condition for both. Perpendicular uses the dot product; parallel uses proportional components.
For part one, perpendicular means the dot product is zero.
So three lambda, minus two, minus six equals zero, giving three lambda equals eight, so lambda is eight thirds.
For part two, parallel means the components are proportional: lambda over three equals two over minus one equals minus three over two.
But two over minus one is minus two, while minus three over two is minus one point five, those are not equal.
Since the last two ratios already disagree, no value of lambda can make the vectors parallel. Recognising that saves you a wild goose chase.
ये example असल में test करती है कि आप जानते हो कि कौन सा product किस condition के साथ जाता है।
हमारे पास a equals lambda i-hat plus two j-hat minus three k-hat, और b equals three i-hat minus j-hat plus two k-hat, और चाहिए lambda perpendicular के लिए, फिर parallel के लिए।
<whisper>यहाँ trap है, students दोनों के लिए same condition उठा लेते हैं। Perpendicular dot product use करता है; parallel proportional components।
Part one के लिए, perpendicular मतलब dot product zero है।
तो three lambda, minus two, minus six equals zero, यानी three lambda equals eight, तो lambda है eight thirds.
Part two के लिए, parallel मतलब components proportional हैं: lambda over three equals two over minus one equals minus three over two.
पर two over minus one है minus two, जबकि minus three over two है minus one point five, वो equal नहीं हैं।
चूँकि आख़िरी दो ratios ही disagree करते हैं, कोई भी lambda vectors को parallel नहीं बना सकता। ये पहचान लेना आपको बेकार की मेहनत से बचा देता है।

sections.title: Example: triangle area and perpendicular unit vector

board_events.text: Example: triangle area and perpendicular unit vector
Sides from vertex A: $\vec a = 3\hat i + \hat j - 2\hat k$, $\vec b = \hat i - 3\hat j + 4\hat k$.
Perpendicular unit vector = $\pm$ (cross product) divided by (its magnitude):
Watch the minus on the $\hat j$ cofactor: $-(12+2) = -14$.

segments.text: This J E E Main level problem puts the cross product to work for both an area and a perpendicular direction.
The two sides from vertex A are a equals three i-hat plus j-hat minus two k-hat, and b equals i-hat minus three j-hat plus four k-hat.

Compute the determinant carefully. The i cofactor is four minus six, minus two; the j cofactor, with its minus sign, is minus the quantity twelve plus two, so minus fourteen; the k cofactor is minus nine minus one, minus ten. So a cross b is minus two i-hat minus fourteen j-hat minus ten k-hat.
Its magnitude is the root of four plus one ninety six plus one hundred, which is root three hundred, or ten root three.
The triangle area is half that magnitude, so five root three square units.
For the perpendicular unit vector, divide the cross product by its magnitude, keeping the plus or minus.
That gives n-hat equals plus or minus one over five root three, times the bracket minus i-hat minus seven j-hat minus five k-hat.
<whisper>And the one thing to watch, the j-hat cofactor carries a minus sign, so minus the quantity twelve plus two is minus fourteen, not plus fourteen.
ये J E E Main level problem cross product को एक area और एक perpendicular direction, दोनों के लिए काम में लाती है।
Vertex A से दो sides हैं a equals three i-hat plus j-hat minus two k-hat, और b equals i-hat minus three j-hat plus four k-hat.

Determinant carefully compute करो। i cofactor है four minus six, minus two; j cofactor, अपने minus sign के साथ, है minus the quantity twelve plus two, तो minus fourteen; k cofactor है minus nine minus one, minus ten. तो a cross b है minus two i-hat minus fourteen j-hat minus ten k-hat.
उसकी magnitude है root of four plus one ninety six plus one hundred, जो root three hundred, या ten root three है।
Triangle area उस magnitude का आधा है, तो five root three square units.
Perpendicular unit vector के लिए, cross product को उसकी magnitude से divide करो, plus or minus रखते हुए।
इससे मिलता है n-hat equals plus or minus one over five root three, times the bracket minus i-hat minus seven j-hat minus five k-hat.
<whisper>और एक चीज़ जो देखनी है, j-hat cofactor minus sign carry करता है, तो minus the quantity twelve plus two है minus fourteen, plus fourteen नहीं।

board_events.text: Example: Lagrange identity and diagonals
Given $|\vec a| = 5$, $|\vec b| = 4$, $\vec a \cdot \vec b = 10$. Find $|\vec a \times \vec b|$ and the parallelogram area from diagonals $\vec a + \vec b$, $\vec a - \vec b$.
Area from diagonals: $\tfrac{1}{2}|\vec d_1 \times \vec d_2|$ with $\vec d_1 = \vec a + \vec b$, $\vec d_2 = \vec a - \vec b$.

board_events.latex: (\vec a + \vec b) \times (\vec a - \vec b) = -2(\vec a \times \vec b)

board_events.text: Lagrange gives $|\vec a \times \vec b|$ with no angle computed at all.

segments.text: A J E E Advanced flavoured problem that shows Lagrange's identity earning its keep.

We are told the magnitude of a is five, the magnitude of b is four, and a dot b is ten, and we must find the magnitude of a cross b, then the area of a parallelogram whose diagonals are a plus b and a minus b.
Apply Lagrange: ten squared plus the magnitude of a cross b, squared, equals twenty five times sixteen, which is four hundred.
So the magnitude of a cross b squared is three hundred, giving the magnitude ten root three, and notice we never touched the angle.
Now the area from diagonals. A parallelogram's area is half the magnitude of the cross product of its two diagonals.
Expand a plus b, crossed with a minus b. The self terms vanish, and using b cross a equals minus a cross b, the whole thing is minus two times a cross b.
So the area is half the magnitude of minus two times a cross b, which is just the magnitude of a cross b, namely ten root three.
<excited>Elegant, the answer circles right back to the cross product magnitude, and Lagrange got us there without a single trig calculation.
एक J E E Advanced flavour वाली problem जो Lagrange's identity को अपनी कीमत साबित करते दिखाती है।
हमें बताया गया magnitude of a है five, magnitude of b है four, और a dot b है ten, और निकालना है magnitude of a cross b, फिर उस parallelogram का area जिसके diagonals हैं a plus b और a minus b.
Lagrange लगाओ: ten squared plus magnitude of a cross b, squared, equals twenty five times sixteen, जो four hundred है।
तो magnitude of a cross b squared है three hundred, यानी magnitude ten root three, और ध्यान दो हमने angle को छुआ तक नहीं।
अब diagonals से area। Parallelogram का area है उसके दो diagonals के cross product की magnitude का आधा।
a plus b को a minus b से cross करके expand करो। Self terms vanish हो जाते हैं, और b cross a equals minus a cross b use करके, पूरी चीज़ है minus two times a cross b.
तो area है minus two times a cross b की magnitude का आधा, जो बस magnitude of a cross b है, यानी ten root three.
<excited>Elegant, answer सीधा cross product magnitude पर वापस घूम आता है, और Lagrange हमें वहाँ बिना एक भी trig calculation के ले गया।

board_events.text: Pitfalls and pro-tips
Dot/cross zero-swap: $\vec a \cdot \vec b = 0$ is perpendicular; $\vec a \times \vec b = \vec 0$ is parallel.
Memorise them as opposites and you will never mix them up.
Projection: divide by the magnitude of the vector you project ONTO, not just the dot.
The determinant's $\hat j$ term carries a minus sign, the commonest cross-product slip.
Cross product is NOT commutative: $\vec a \times \vec b = -\,\vec b \times \vec a$.
Pro-tip: the sign of the dot product reads the angle: $+$ acute, $0$ right, $-$ obtuse.
A negative projection must pair with a negative dot product, an instant MCQ check.

segments.text: Let me close the two products with the traps that cost marks, and the pro-tip that saves them.
The biggest one is the zero-condition swap: a dot b equal to zero means perpendicular, while a cross b equal to the zero vector means parallel.
Memorise those two as exact opposites, and you will never mix them up again.
Second, in a projection, always divide by the magnitude of the vector you are projecting onto, do not stop at the bare dot product.
Third, the determinant's j-hat term carries a minus sign; that lone minus is the most common cross-product slip in exams.
Fourth, keep the cross product's order, it is not commutative, so a cross b equals minus b cross a, and swapping matters when direction matters.
And now the pro-tip that pays off instantly: the sign of the dot product reads the angle for you, positive is acute, zero is a right angle, negative is obtuse.
<excited>So a negative projection must pair with a negative dot product; if an option breaks that, eliminate it on sight.
दोनों products को उन traps के साथ close करते हैं जो marks खाते हैं, और वो pro-tip जो उन्हें बचाती है।
सबसे बड़ा है zero-condition swap: a dot b equal to zero मतलब perpendicular, जबकि a cross b equal to zero vector मतलब parallel।
इन दोनों को exact opposites की तरह याद कर लो, और आप कभी mix नहीं करोगे।
दूसरा, projection में, हमेशा उस vector की magnitude से divide करो जिस पर project कर रहे हो, bare dot product पर मत रुको।
तीसरा, determinant का j-hat term minus sign carry करता है; वो अकेला minus exams में सबसे common cross-product slip है।
चौथा, cross product का order रखो, ये commutative नहीं है, तो a cross b equals minus b cross a, और जहाँ direction matter करे वहाँ swap matter करता है।
और अब वो pro-tip जो instantly pay off करती है: dot product का sign आपके लिए angle पढ़ देता है, positive acute है, zero right angle है, negative obtuse है।
<excited>तो negative projection को negative dot product के साथ pair होना ही चाहिए; अगर कोई option ये तोड़े, देखते ही eliminate।
